pos: n. (a Levite of the house of Rehabiah, named in the courses David set over the sanctuary)
etymology: Hebrew Yishshiyyah, the LORD lendeth, or whom the LORD lendeth, from the root shaah with the divine name Yah; named twice, 1 Chronicles 24:21 and 24:25.
biblical_def: Isshiah is a Levite who exists in Scripture only inside a list. He appears in the chapter where David, near the end of his reign, divided the sons of Levi into courses for the house of the LORD: “Concerning Rehabiah: of the sons of Rehabiah, the first was Isshiah” (1 Chronicles 24:21), and again four verses later, “The brother of Michah was Isshiah: of the sons of Isshiah; Zechariah” (1 Chronicles 24:25). Nothing else is told of him — no deed, no word, no death. What the Chronicler is doing with him is nevertheless plain. The lots were cast “one principal household being taken for Eleazar, and one taken for Ithamar” (1 Chronicles 24:6), so that the order of service in the temple was not settled by rank or preference but by the hand of God upon a lot. Isshiah's name is in that record because the worship of God is ordered worship, and ordered worship requires that actual men be named and actually assigned. The Levites “were numbered from the age of thirty years and upward” (1 Chronicles 23:3), counted and set to their charge. A man whose whole biblical biography is a place in a roster still has a place in the house of God, and the Holy Ghost saw fit to write it down.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Isshiah, a Hebrew proper name signifying the LORD lendeth; a Levite of the sons of Rehabiah, named in the courses of the sanctuary in 1 Chronicles 24.
webster_full: Hebrew Yishshiyyah, the LORD lendeth, or whom Jehovah lendeth.
Compounded of a verbal root signifying to lend or to give, with Yah, the covenant name of God.
It occurs twice in the Authorized Version, both in 1 Chronicles 24.
He is reckoned among the sons of Rehabiah, of the house of Levi.
His son is given as Zechariah, 1 Chronicles 24:25.
scriptures: Concerning Rehabiah: of the sons of Rehabiah, the first was Isshiah.
The brother of Michah was Isshiah: of the sons of Isshiah; Zechariah.
Now the Levites were numbered from the age of thirty years and upward: and their number by their polls, man by man, was thirty and eight thousand.

And Shemaiah the son of Nethaneel the scribe, one of the Levites, wrote them before the king, and the princes, and Zadok the priest, and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, and before the chief of the fathers of the priests and Levites: one principal household being taken for Eleazar, and one taken for Ithamar.
corruption_summary: A name in a roster is counted worthless by an age that measures worth by visibility; Scripture counts the roster itself an act of worship.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct skips the genealogies. A man with no narrative is assumed to have no significance, and the chapters that name him are treated as archive rather than Scripture. But the Chronicler wrote these lists after the exile, to a people who needed to know that the service of God had an order and that they belonged to it. Isshiah is named so that the house of Rehabiah could be found again. The list is pastoral, not clerical.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps records of men who keep no records of themselves. Every one of these Levites served out his course and died, and the only monument is a line in a chapter most readers pass over. That is enough. “The Lord knoweth them that are his” (2 Timothy 2:19), and the naming of Isshiah in a list David drew up is a small, early witness to it.

pos: n. (a Levite of the sons of Shubael; also the Meronothite who kept David's asses)
etymology: Hebrew Yechdeyahu, union of the LORD, or whom the LORD maketh glad, from chadah, to rejoice, with Yah; named twice, 1 Chronicles 24:20 and 27:30.
biblical_def: Jehdeiah is named twice, and the two notices are of two different men doing two different kinds of work for the same king. The first is a Levite: “And the rest of the sons of Levi were these: Of the sons of Amram; Shubael: of the sons of Shubael; Jehdeiah” (1 Chronicles 24:20). The second is an officer of David's estate: “Over the camels also was Obil the Ishmaelite: and over the asses was Jehdeiah the Meronothite” (1 Chronicles 27:30). That second list is one of the most unglamorous passages in Scripture — the men set over David's herds, vineyards, oliveyards, cellars and storehouses — and it is written with the same care as the roll of his mighty men. The Chronicler sets the sanctuary courses and the king's asses within a few chapters of each other and does not apologise for either. A kingdom under God has both: men who stand before the ark, and men who see that the beasts are fed. “All these the sons of Jediael, by the heads of their fathers” (1 Chronicles 7:11) is the register's ordinary voice, and Jehdeiah belongs to it twice over.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Jehdeiah, a Hebrew proper name signifying union of the LORD; borne by a Levite of the sons of Shubael, and by the Meronothite set over David's asses.
webster_full: Hebrew Yechdeyahu, union of the LORD, or whom Jehovah maketh glad.

scriptures: And the rest of the sons of Levi were these: Of the sons of Amram; Shubael: of the sons of Shubael; Jehdeiah.

All these the sons of Jediael, by the heads of their fathers, mighty men of valour, were seventeen thousand and two hundred soldiers, fit to go out for war and battle.
And over the flocks was Jaziz the Hagerite. All these were the rulers of the substance which was king David's.
corruption_summary: Work is graded by its visibility; Scripture grades it by whose it is, and sets the sanctuary roster and the royal herdsmen in the same book.
corruption_paragraphs: A culture that sorts labour into meaningful and menial would file the man over the asses well below the man over the courses of the sanctuary. The Chronicler files them in the same register, under the same king, in the same reign, and gives the herdsman his own clause. Nothing in the text suggests that the second Jehdeiah was serving God less than the first.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that every lawful calling is a station under God, and that faithfulness in it is the whole requirement. “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). The asses of David were real property with real care owed them, and a man's name is in the word of God because he saw to them.

pos: n. (the fourth son of Hebron the Levite, named in the courses of David)
etymology: Hebrew Yeqam'am, the kinsman will raise up, or let the people rise, from qum, to rise or stand, with am, a people; named twice, 1 Chronicles 23:19 and 24:23.
biblical_def: Jekameam is the fourth of the four sons of Hebron, a Levite of the house of Kohath, and he is named twice in identical order: “Of the sons of Hebron; Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth” (1 Chronicles 23:19), then “And the sons of Hebron; Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, Jekameam the fourth” (1 Chronicles 24:23). The repetition is the point. These are two distinct registers — the numbering of the Levites for the service of the house of the LORD, and the division of the sons of Levi by lot — and in both the same four men stand in the same rank. The order of a Levitical house was not re-shuffled from one census to the next; it was fixed and it was honoured. His name means that the people may rise, and that is precisely the office of the Levite: to stand so that Israel may stand. “Because their office was to wait on the sons of Aaron for the service of the house of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 23:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): Jekameam, a Hebrew proper name signifying the people shall rise, or the kinsman gathers; the fourth son of Hebron the Levite in 1 Chronicles 23 and 24.
webster_full: Hebrew Yeqam'am, let the people rise, or the kinsman will raise up.
From qum, to rise, stand, or be established, with am, a people or kindred.

He is reckoned fourth among the sons of Hebron, of the Kohathites.
The same four brethren stand in the same order in both lists.
scriptures: Of the sons of Hebron; Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.

And that they should keep the charge of the tabernacle of the congregation, and the charge of the holy place, and the charge of the sons of Aaron their brethren, in the service of the house of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Repetition in Scripture is read as redundancy; here it is testimony that the order God appointed did not shift between one register and the next.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical reading treats a list that occurs twice as evidence of clumsy compilation. The Chronicler is doing something else. He gives the Hebronites once under the numbering of the Levites for service, and once under the casting of lots for their courses, and the four names stand in unbroken order both times, because the house of God is not governed by improvisation.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the regulative principle of worship in its plainest form: God appoints the service, God appoints the servants, and men do not reorder what He has set. “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40). Jekameam was fourth, and remained fourth, and that is written twice so that nobody would move him.

pos: n. (a Levite of the sons of Laadan, set with his brother over the treasures of the house of the LORD)
etymology: Hebrew Zetham, an olive, or olive-shining, from the same root as zayith, an olive tree; named twice, 1 Chronicles 23:8 and 26:22.
biblical_def: Zetham is a Gershonite Levite of the family of Laadan: “The sons of Laadan; the chief was Jehiel, and Zetham, and Joel, three” (1 Chronicles 23:8). Three chapters later his charge is given: “The sons of Jehieli; Zetham, and Joel his brother, which were over the treasures of the house of the LORD” (1 Chronicles 26:22). The treasuries held what Israel had dedicated — spoil won in battle, gifts of the princes, the silver and gold given for the house that Solomon would build. Men had to be set over it who would not touch it. The Chronicler names them, because an office with money in it is an office that must have a name attached. Samuel the seer, Saul, Abner and Joab had all dedicated things to the treasuries (1 Chronicles 26:28), and the keeping of those things was a trust held before God and before Israel. Zetham's name means an olive, the tree of oil and of the lamp, and he was set where the oil was stored.

Which Shelomith and his brethren were over all the treasures of the dedicated things, which David the king, and the chief fathers, the captains over thousands and hundreds, and the captains of the host, had dedicated.

And all that Samuel the seer, and Saul the son of Kish, and Abner the son of Ner, and Joab the son of Zeruiah, had dedicated; and whosoever had dedicated any thing, it was under the hand of Shelomith, and of his brethren.
corruption_summary: Handling the treasury of God's house is treated as administration; Scripture treats it as a sacred trust with names written beside it.
corruption_paragraphs: Where money is concerned, modern practice prefers systems to names: anonymous committees, pooled responsibility, no one person answerable. The Chronicler does the opposite. He names Zetham and Joel and says exactly what they were over. Dedicated things carry the name of the man who keeps them, because that is the only arrangement under which a theft is also a betrayal.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is accountability by name in the handling of what belongs to God. Paul kept the same rule in the collection for Jerusalem, “Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men” (2 Corinthians 8:21). A church treasury with no named steward is not humble; it is unguarded.

pos: n. (chief of the Hebronites in the fortieth year of David; called Jeriah in the earlier lists)
etymology: Hebrew Yeriyyahu, the LORD doth found, or taught of the LORD, from yarah, to throw, cast or teach, with Yah; the fuller form of Jeriah, 1 Chronicles 26:31.
biblical_def: Jerijah is the first-named of the four sons of Hebron, and the Authorized Version gives his name in two forms: Jeriah in the registers of the courses, and Jerijah where his office is described. “Among the Hebronites was Jerijah the chief, even among the Hebronites, according to the generations of his fathers. In the fortieth year of the reign of David they were sought for, and there were found among them mighty men of valour at Jazer of Gilead” (1 Chronicles 26:31). The fortieth year is David's last. At the end of a reign, when a king might reasonably leave matters as they stood, a search was made through the Hebronite houses, and men fit for service were found east of Jordan, far from Jerusalem. They were set over Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh “for every matter pertaining to God, and affairs of the king” (1 Chronicles 26:32). Jerijah stands at the head of that reckoning: a Levite chief whose brethren were sought out, counted, and sent to the far side of the river to keep both church and commonwealth in order.

He was chief among the Hebronites, a Kohathite house of Levi.

And his brethren, men of valour, were two thousand and seven hundred chief fathers, whom king David made rulers over the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half tribe of Manasseh, for every matter pertaining to God, and affairs of the king.

corruption_summary: A long tenure is expected to coast at its end; David in his fortieth year sent men out to search the Levitical houses and staff the far provinces.
corruption_paragraphs: The last year of a reign invites neglect: the work is handed to a successor, and the outlying regions are the first to be let go. 1 Chronicles 26 records the opposite. In the fortieth year, men were sought for among the Hebronites, mighty men of valour were found at Jazer of Gilead, and two thousand seven hundred chief fathers were set over the tribes beyond Jordan.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an office is to be discharged to the last day of it. “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might” (Ecclesiastes 9:10). David was old, and he ordered the Levites, the gatekeepers, the treasuries and the Transjordan oversight, and then he died. Jerijah's name belongs to the final act of a faithful administration.

pos: n. (an overseer of the dedicated things under Hezekiah's reformation)
etymology: Hebrew Yismakyahu, the LORD sustaineth, or whom the LORD upholds, from samak, to lean upon or uphold, with Yah; named once, 2 Chronicles 31:13.
biblical_def: Ismachiah appears once, in the middle of Hezekiah's reformation, as one of ten men appointed to handle the offerings the revived nation brought in: “And Jehiel, and Azaziah, and Nahath, and Asahel, and Jerimoth, and Jozabad, and Eliel, and Ismachiah, and Mahath, and Benaiah, were overseers under the hand of Cononiah and Shimei his brother, at the commandment of Hezekiah the king, and Azariah the ruler of the house of God” (2 Chronicles 31:13). The occasion is worth marking. When Hezekiah commanded the people to give the portion of the priests and Levites, “as soon as the commandment came abroad, the children of Israel brought in abundance the firstfruits” (2 Chronicles 31:5), and the heaps grew so large that chambers had to be prepared in the house of the LORD. Revival produced goods, and goods required overseers, and overseers required names. Ismachiah is one of ten men whose only recorded act is to have been trustworthy with other people's tithes. His name means the LORD sustains, and he was set over the means by which the LORD sustained His ministers.

corruption_summary: Reformation is imagined as preaching alone; Scripture shows it producing tithes, storehouses, chambers and ten named men to keep the accounts.
corruption_paragraphs: Accounts of revival tend to end at the sermon and the response. 2 Chronicles 31 keeps going: the people bring in firstfruits in abundance, the heaps lie in the courts from the third month to the seventh, chambers are prepared, and a named administration is appointed to distribute to the priests and Levites in their cities. Hezekiah did not leave the aftermath to goodwill.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that genuine reformation shows up in the ledger. “And thus did Hezekiah throughout all Judah, and wrought that which was good and right and truth before the LORD his God” (2 Chronicles 31:20). A people who will not fund the ministry of the word have not been reformed by it, and a ministry that will not be accountable for the funds has not understood the reformation either.

pos: n. (the eighth son of Obed-edom among the porters of the house of the LORD)
etymology: Hebrew Pe'ullethay, wages of the LORD, or my work is of Jehovah, from pe'ullah, work, wages or recompence; named once, 1 Chronicles 26:5.
biblical_def: Peulthai is the eighth and last-named son of Obed-edom, and the verse that names him gives the reason for the whole family: “Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, Peulthai the eighth: for God blessed him” (1 Chronicles 26:5). The blessing is a particular one with a history behind it. When the ark of God was carried aside into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite after the death of Uzza, “the LORD blessed Obededom, and all his household” (2 Samuel 6:11). Eight sons are the shape that blessing took, and those sons became porters, keepers of the gates of the house they had once kept in their own home. Peulthai's name means the wages, or the recompence, of the LORD — a last son in a list of blessing, named for the reward. The Chronicler adds of this house, “All these of the sons of Obededom: they and their sons and their brethren, able men for strength for the service, were threescore and two of Obededom” (1 Chronicles 26:8). One household's three months of hospitality to the ark became sixty-two men in the service of the sanctuary.

corruption_summary: Blessing is read as sentiment or circumstance; here it is counted in sons, named one by one, and traced to a specific act of reverence toward the ark.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern talk of being blessed attaches the word to a mood or a run of good fortune. The Chronicler uses it as a causal statement with evidence attached: eight sons are listed, and then the clause, for God blessed him. The reader is expected to remember three months during which a Gittite housed the ark that had just struck Uzza dead, and to see the household that grew out of it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is no man's debtor, and that reverence shown Him in a dangerous hour is repaid in kind and in time. “them that honour me I will honour” (1 Samuel 2:30). Obed-edom kept the ark; his sons kept the gates; and the last of them was called the recompence of the LORD.

pos: n. (a Gershonite Levite in the descent of Asaph's house)
etymology: Hebrew Ye'atheray, steadfast, or whom the LORD leads; named once, 1 Chronicles 6:21.
biblical_def: Jeaterai stands at the end of a short descent in the Levitical genealogy of Gershom: “Joah his son, Iddo his son, Zerah his son, Jeaterai his son” (1 Chronicles 6:21). Four men, four words apiece, and the line stops. The chapter around him is one of the longest unbroken genealogies in Scripture, running the sons of Levi down through the priesthood to the captivity, and then running the singers back up from Heman to Levi to Israel. Its purpose is stated plainly: these are they “whom David set over the service of song in the house of the LORD, after that the ark had rest” (1 Chronicles 6:31). Jeaterai is in the ancestry of that ministry. He sang nothing that is recorded and said nothing that is recorded, but the men who led Israel's praise could trace their descent through him, and in a house where the right to serve ran by birth, that mattered. Of the returning exiles who could not find their register it is written, “therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” (Ezra 2:62). A name like Jeaterai is the reason others were not.

These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood.
corruption_summary: Genealogy is dismissed as tribal bookkeeping; in Israel it was the title deed to a ministry, and a man without it lost his place.
corruption_paragraphs: A reader trained to skip the registers misses what they were for. Under the law the right to serve at the altar and in the song was inherited, not claimed, and the proof was a written descent. Ezra records men who sought their register among those reckoned by genealogy, could not find it, and were put from the priesthood until a priest should stand up with Urim and Thummim. The lists were not antiquarian; they were legal.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's appointments to office are objective and traceable, not self-asserted. The New Testament keeps the same instinct in a new key: “And no man taketh this honour unto himself, but he that is called of God, as was Aaron” (Hebrews 5:4). Jeaterai's one line is part of somebody's warrant to sing.

pos: n. pl. (the Levitical family descended from Shimei son of Gershon)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Shim'i, the Shimeite, a patronymic from Shim'i, Shimei, itself from shama, to hear; named once, Numbers 3:21.
biblical_def: The Shimites are one of the two families into which the house of Gershon divided: “Of Gershon was the family of the Libnites, and the family of the Shimites: these are the families of the Gershonites” (Numbers 3:21). Their charge in the wilderness is given a few verses later — “the tabernacle, and the tent, the covering thereof, and the hanging for the door of the tabernacle of the congregation” (Numbers 3:25) — that is, the fabric of the dwelling itself, the curtains and coverings and the door-hanging, carried on wagons behind the camp. They pitched westward, behind the tabernacle. The numbering of this house was “seven thousand and five hundred” males from a month old and upward (Numbers 3:22). What the passage establishes is that the Levites were not a crowd of volunteers but an ordered body with named families, assigned loads, fixed stations and a counted strength. The tabernacle moved through the wilderness because particular clans carried particular parts of it, and the Shimites carried the tent.

webster_full: Hebrew ha-Shim'i, the Shimeite, used collectively of the family.

corruption_summary: Dividing labour by family is read as an accident of ancient society; in the camp it was divine appointment, and the loads were assigned by name.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern eye reads tribal allotment as mere custom and reaches for a sociological explanation of it. Numbers 3 gives a different account: the LORD spoke to Moses, the Levites were taken instead of the firstborn, and each family received a charge from Him. The Gershonites did not choose the curtains; they were given them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God distributes service as He pleases, and the part assigned is the part to be carried. Paul reasons from the same premise: “But now hath God set the members every one of them in the body, as it hath pleased him” (1 Corinthians 12:18). A family that carried coverings for forty years never touched the ark, and was not thereby of less account in the camp.

pos: n. pl. (the family of Machir son of Manasseh, numbered in the plains of Moab)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Makiri, the Machirite, a patronymic from Makir, Machir, sold or a salesman, from makar, to sell; named once, Numbers 26:29.
biblical_def: The Machirites are named in the second numbering of Israel, taken in the plains of Moab before the land was divided: “Of the sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the family of the Machirites: and Machir begat Gilead: of Gilead come the family of the Gileadites” (Numbers 26:29). The verse is a hinge. The census of Numbers 26 was taken expressly for the inheritance — “Unto these the land shall be divided for an inheritance according to the number of names” (Numbers 26:53) — and the Machirites are the house through which Manasseh's portion east of Jordan came. Machir was the firstborn of Manasseh, “a man of war, therefore he had Gilead and Bashan” (Joshua 17:1). The family had a hard border to hold and held it. Deborah sang of them in the day of Barak: “out of Machir came down governors” (Judges 5:14). A clan name in a census list turns out to be the warrant for a territory, a line of rulers, and a share in the song of a victory.

corruption_summary: A census is treated as a tool of the state; in Numbers 26 it is the instrument by which God gives every family its named and measured inheritance.
corruption_paragraphs: Counting people carries a suspicion in modern thought, and not without cause — David's numbering brought a plague. But Numbers 26 is commanded, and its purpose is stated: the land shall be divided according to the number of names. The count exists so that no household is left out and no household takes more than its portion. It protects the weak clan from the strong one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that inheritance in Scripture is particular, bounded and given, not seized. The Machirites were men of war who received Gilead, and the record of what they received is written down so that later generations could not quietly enlarge it. “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Proverbs 22:28).
